questions.question: Describe the results of testing a tray of metal objects with a magnet, explain the terms ferrous and non-ferrous, and account for the tin can and galvanised wire.
questions.expected_answer: Steel nails, washers, the food tin, galvanised wire and most stainless steel are attracted; copper wire, the aluminium can, the brass key and the lead sinker are not. Metals containing iron, nickel or cobalt, chiefly steel, are attracted and are called ferrous, from ferrum, the Latin for iron; copper, aluminium, brass, lead, zinc, gold and silver are non-ferrous and are ignored. The tin can is steel with a thin tin coating and the galvanised wire is steel coated with zinc; tin and zinc are non-magnetic but the magnetic force passes through the thin coating to the steel beneath, so both stick. Appearance and names are unreliable; only the test decides.

questions.question: Explain, using the idea of domains, why iron is attracted to a magnet while copper is not, and why size does not change whether an object is attracted.
questions.expected_answer: Iron, nickel and cobalt contain tiny regions called domains that each act as a small magnet; in an unmagnetised nail they point in all directions and cancel. A nearby magnet makes the domains line up with its field, turning the nail into a temporary magnet whose near end is the opposite pole, so it is attracted; when the magnet is removed most domains relax. Copper and aluminium have no domains, so nothing lines up and there is nothing to pull. Because the property belongs to the material, a steel washer and a steel girder are both ferrous and a speck of copper and a copper roof are both non-ferrous; size affects only how strongly a piece can be held.

questions.question: Describe how to record a fair materials test and write its conclusion, and state what magnetic sorting cannot do for the scrap dealer.
questions.expected_answer: Rule a table with columns for object, metal, prediction, result and note; test every object with the same pole at the same distance and lift the same way, twice, and write surprises and their explanations in the note column. Conclude in two sentences: metals containing iron, nickel or cobalt, mainly steel, are ferrous and attracted; copper, aluminium, brass, lead and zinc are non-ferrous and not attracted, so a magnet can separate ferrous from non-ferrous scrap. The conclusion links the result to the scenario. Its limit is that a magnet cannot separate copper from aluminium or one steel from another, so the non-ferrous pile needs another sorting method.
